opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it came from where I started. I spent years in research, building Taichi as a programming language for graphics and simulation, and in that world, if you understand the problem deeply and write good code, you can make real progress. So when I started the company, I assumed running it would be a similar kind of problem: hard, but something I could reason through from first principles.

What I didn't realize was that most of the difficulty isn't technical at all. It's people, it's timing, it's figuring out who your customer actually is and what they'll pay for. It's hiring, managing expectations, raising money, and making decisions with very incomplete information. None of that showed up in my PhD. I knew compilers and physics simulation very well, but I'd never managed a team, never sold anything, never had to think about cash flow.

There's a well-known pattern where the less you know about a field, the less you're aware of what you're missing. I was confident because I'd succeeded in one domain and quietly assumed the skills would transfer. Some did, like persistence and learning quickly, but a lot didn't.

So looking back, I don't see it as stupidity, more as a natural blind spot for a technical founder. The lesson for me was to be much more humble when entering a new domain, to look for people who've actually done it and listen to them, and to accept that I'd be a beginner again. That's uncomfortable when you're used to being the expert in the room, but I think it's the only way to really grow.

r001.rationale: He says confidence from success in research led him to assume his skills would transfer, then identifies greater humility as the lesson—attributing his blind spot to insufficient humility.

r002.rationale: He describes what he learned in retrospect, but does not say he promptly changed course after recognizing he was wrong.

r003.rationale: He does not discuss prior executive experience at a large company or say it fails to spare founders from startup difficulties.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the failure came from a kind of overconfidence that academia quietly trains into you. When I was doing my PhD at MIT, I had just built Taichi, I had written papers that people were citing, I had a sense that if I could understand something as hard as differentiable physics simulation, I could understand anything. Running a company felt like it would be another problem to solve, maybe a harder one, but the same kind of problem.

That turned out to be completely wrong, and it took me a while to see why. In research, the feedback loop is clean. You have a hypothesis, you run the experiment, the GPU tells you whether you're right. The ground truth exists and you can usually find it. In a company, most of the important questions have no ground truth at all. Should we build for developers or for enterprises? Should we hire this person? Is this customer telling us what they actually need or what they think they need? You make the decision, and then reality takes a year to give you a very noisy answer, and by then you've made fifty other decisions on top of it.

So my first mistake was treating management as an engineering problem. I remember thinking, if I just design the right process, the right org structure, the right OKRs, the company will run like a well-written program. And of course people are not functions. They have emotions, they have ambitions, they misunderstand each other, they get tired. I was a good programmer and a very bad people person at the beginning, and I didn't even know that was a separate skill.

The second thing is that I underestimated how much I didn't know about things that looked trivial from the outside. Sales, for example. I thought selling was just explaining the technology well. It's not. It's understanding someone else's problem deeply enough that they trust you to solve it. Fundraising, hiring, pricing, all of these looked simple because I had never done them, and simple-looking things that you've never done are the most dangerous ones.

What I think now, with some distance, is that the failure to recognize my ignorance wasn't really a character flaw, it was structural. Nobody around me in academia could tell me, because they didn't know either. And the people who did know, experienced founders, operators, I didn't seek them out early enough because I didn't think I needed them. The lesson I'd give to anyone coming from research is this: the thing you're best at will give you confidence, and that confidence will leak into domains where it has no basis. Be very suspicious when something feels easy and you've never done it before. That feeling is almost always a sign that you're missing something, not that you've figured it out.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his initial blind spot to overconfidence and says he did not seek experienced founders because he thought he did not need them.

r002.rationale: It says it took him a while to understand why he was wrong; it does not say he promptly changed course.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss prior executive experience at a large company or whether it prepares founders for startup difficulties.

I assumed running a company would work in a similar way. But building a product, understanding customers, and helping a team work together require different kinds of judgment. Initially, I didn’t even have enough experience to recognize those gaps. Looking back, the mistake wasn’t simply lacking knowledge; it was being too confident that the way I already knew how to solve problems would be enough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I didn’t know what I didn’t know. My background was technical, so I was used to problems where, if I worked hard enough and understood the details, I could find a solution. I carried that mindset into starting a company without realizing how much I still had to learn about customers, hiring, and building a business.

Looking back, the mistake wasn’t simply lacking experience. It was assuming that my experience in one area would transfer so easily to another. I needed to ask more questions and recognize the limits of my own judgment.
